subtopics.title: Pitch, loudness, amplitude and intensity
subtopics.learning_goal: Frequency determines the fundamental pitch of a simple tone, amplitude measures oscillation magnitude, and mean intensity in a fixed medium for a linear sinusoidal plane wave depends on the square of pressure amplitude.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Reconstruct two pressure-time graphs from extrema and interval data, preserving their unequal amplitudes and frequencies, then compare intensity under common impedance.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Trace A repeats an upward zero crossing every 4 ms and has peak-to-peak pressure 6 Pa. Trace B has successive pressure maxima 2 ms apart and peak-to-peak 3 Pa. Draw one full cycle of each on common scales; compare pitch and intensity in the same medium. Shortest valid route: A: f=250 Hz, peak 3 Pa. B: f=500 Hz, peak 1.5 Pa. B higher pitch, intensity A/B=4. Show A crossing upward at t=0 and B maximum at t=0 if choosing those reference points.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Identify pressure field and common medium.

representation_translation.evidence: Convert extrema and phase intervals into two scaled graphs.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Calculate frequency and amplitude before pressure-intensity comparison.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Peak-to-peak is not peak; slope crossings must match phase.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Choose between ideal spherical spreading and an altered power-loss model using measurements at multiple distances.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: At 2 m and 4 m from a source, a calibrated pressure sensor reports peak amplitudes 8 and 4 Pa. At 8 m it reports 1 Pa. Test ideal isotropic lossless spreading in one medium and infer what the data do and do not establish. Shortest valid route: First pair fits p∝1/r. Ideal prediction at 8 m is 2 Pa, observed 1 Pa; intensity one-quarter of ideal at 8 m. Some assumption fails; cannot uniquely identify absorption, directivity or reflections from these data.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Competing spreading and additional-loss models must be tested.

representation_translation.evidence: Map sensor amplitude readings into power ratios.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Predict readings from two positions and test a third.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Additional loss or directivity defeats inverse-square claim.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Determine whether mixed pressure and displacement evidence uniquely establishes intensity ordering, and construct physically compatible countermodels under unknown impedance or frequency.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: A displacement trace for tone A has twice the displacement amplitude of tone B but half its frequency. Both are progressive linear waves. The medium for each is not specified. A report claims IA>IB and A must sound louder. Decide whether the evidence proves either claim; use I∝ρv(fA_displacement)² and construct two compatible impedance cases with opposite intensity order. Shortest valid route: Products fA_displacement equal, so IA/IB=(ρv)A/(ρv)B. If impedance ratio is 2, IA>IB; if 1/2, IA<IB; equal impedances give equal intensity. Loudness additionally depends on frequency and listener. Measure each impedance or pressure and impedance.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Distinguish displacement, pressure and subjective loudness as distinct models.

representation_translation.evidence: Coordinate sensor quantities and frequency/impedance dependencies rather than compare graph heights.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Establish conditional intensity ordering, construct contrasting parameter cases, specify a discriminating measurement.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Unknown impedance or frequency reverses an otherwise plausible ordering.

science_records.claim: Frequency determines the fundamental pitch of a simple tone, amplitude measures oscillation magnitude, and mean intensity in a fixed medium for a linear sinusoidal plane wave depends on the square of pressure amplitude.
science_records.law_or_model: f=1/T; A=(maximum−minimum)/2 for symmetric sinusoid; I=p_rms²/(ρv) = p_peak²/(2ρv); I=P/(4πr²) only for an ideal isotropic source
assumptions: Sinusoidal signals and calibrated linear sensors for peak-to-peak inference; use the appropriate zero/reference level.
Pressure squared intensity relation assumes a progressive linear wave and common impedance ρv when comparing.
conditions_and_limits: Sinusoidal signals and calibrated linear sensors for peak-to-peak inference; use the appropriate zero/reference level.
Pressure squared intensity relation assumes a progressive linear wave and common impedance ρv when comparing.
Inverse-square spreading assumes isotropic point-like source, negligible absorption/reflections, far from near-field effects.
Loudness is not determined by intensity ratio alone; avoid hearing-risk experiments and use hypothetical data.
science_records.units_and_signs: f in Hz, displacement amplitude in m, pressure amplitude in Pa, intensity in W/m²; loudness is perceptual, not identical to intensity.

core1a.phenomenon: Two sounds can have the same pitch but different measured amplitude and perceived loudness.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
A vibrating source produces an oscillation; a sensor may record displacement, pressure, or an electrical signal proportional to one of them. In a symmetric sinusoid, amplitude is the maximum deviation from the equilibrium value, half the peak-to-peak span. A graph's horizontal repeat interval determines period and frequency. A tall graph does not imply a higher frequency. Pitch describes perception of frequency (especially the fundamental of a simple tone), whereas loudness depends on intensity, frequency sensitivity, duration, listening conditions and the listener.

Sound intensity is the average power transported per unit area normal to propagation. For a linear progressive sinusoidal plane wave in the same medium, mean intensity is I=p_rms²/(ρv), where p_rms is the root-mean-square excess pressure, ρ is density and v is sound speed. For a sinusoid p_rms=p_peak/√2. Thus two matched pressure measurements in the same medium have intensity ratio (p₁/p₂)². Pressure and displacement amplitudes are not interchangeable. In the same medium a displacement amplitude A gives pressure amplitude proportional to fA for a linear travelling sinusoid; comparing different frequencies by displacement amplitude alone is insufficient. The latter relations are explicitly enrichment, not asserted compulsory.

A separate geometric model applies to an ideal isotropic source in an unbounded lossless medium: power crosses a spherical area 4πr², so intensity P/(4πr²). That is an inverse-square relation, not a rule that all spaces or sources obey. Under those conditions and a fixed medium, pressure amplitude is proportional to 1/r. In rooms, reflections, directivity, absorption or interference can defeat this model. If two different-frequency tones are averaged over sufficiently long intervals, their mean intensities may be added when cross terms average out; coherent same-frequency waves cannot always be treated that way.

The reasoning job is to decide what the sensor measured, separate frequency from amplitude, and select a propagation model supported by the conditions. A ratio of pressures is not a ratio of powers. A ratio of intensities does not establish the ratio of perceived loudness. The existing Core2 sound-wave candidate requires interpreting displacement amplitude; this unit prepares that prerequisite and extends it with original advanced intensity comparisons.

derivation_steps.action: Read the graph's vertical physical quantity and equilibrium baseline.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Amplitude must describe a specified field; pressure, displacement and voltage are different quantities.

derivation_steps.action: Recover period from matching phase and separate it from amplitude.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Frequency uses temporal repetition, not vertical height.

derivation_steps.action: Select pressure-intensity or geometric spreading model under its explicit conditions.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Energy transported per area and wave impedance govern the pressure relation; conservation through spheres gives ideal spreading.

derivation_steps.action: Check a second observation or identify missing perceptual/medium information.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A numerical intensity does not uniquely establish perceived loudness.

model_limits: Sinusoidal signals and calibrated linear sensors for peak-to-peak inference; use the appropriate zero/reference level.
Pressure squared intensity relation assumes a progressive linear wave and common impedance ρv when comparing.
Inverse-square spreading assumes isotropic point-like source, negligible absorption/reflections, far from near-field effects.
Loudness is not determined by intensity ratio alone; avoid hearing-risk experiments and use hypothetical data.

progressive_examples.problem: A sinusoidal pressure trace has extrema +3 Pa and −3 Pa with a period of 5 ms. Find peak pressure and f.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Peak-to-peak is 6 Pa; the full cycle repeats five milliseconds later.

progressive_examples.problem: Two sinusoidal waves in the same medium have peak pressures 2 and 6 Pa. Compare their intensities.
progressive_examples.independent_check: RMS pressure ratio is also 3, so square gives 9.

progressive_examples.problem: An ideal isotropic source gives intensity 0.08 W/m² at 2 m. Find intensity at 4 m and pressure-amplitude ratio.
progressive_examples.reasoning: I(4)=0.02 W/m²; p(4)/p(2)=1/2 in the same medium.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Intensity multiplied by spherical area is constant at both locations.

figures.reasoning_step: Frequency and pressure amplitude are separate
figures.scene_description: Two sinusoidal pressure traces have equal time period and different heights. Original inline SVG, not source examination figure.

misconception.wrong_model: Taller wave graphs have higher pitch; twice the pressure amplitude means twice the intensity or twice the perceived loudness.
misconception.diagnostic: Compare two equal-period pressure traces with different amplitudes. Which measurements alone are enough to rank frequency, intensity and perception?
misconception.repair: Read independent graph dimensions, square pressure ratio under matched impedance and keep perceptual claims conditional.

exit_check.task: Two same-frequency waves have pressure peak-to-peak values 8 Pa and 12 Pa in one medium. Compare intensity.
exit_check.reasoning: Peak amplitudes 4 and 6 Pa; squared ratio (6/4)².

core1b.fresh_task: Trace X has pressure maximum 5 Pa and minimum −5 Pa, maxima 5 ms apart. Y has extrema ±2.5 Pa, maxima 2.5 ms apart. Construct both graphs on a common time/pressure grid and compare f and mean intensity.
core1b.protected_work: Reconstruct two pressure-time graphs from extrema and interval data, preserving their unequal amplitudes and frequencies, then compare intensity under common impedance.

stages.predict: Predict which trace, X or Y, has the higher pitch and which has higher intensity. Record both initial judgements.
stages.attempt: Trace X has pressure maximum 5 Pa and minimum −5 Pa, maxima 5 ms apart. Y has extrema ±2.5 Pa, maxima 2.5 ms apart. Construct both graphs on a common time/pressure grid and compare f and mean intensity.
stages.reconstruct: fX=200, fY=400 Hz; amplitudes 5,2.5 Pa. IX/IY=4 at common impedance. Mark two Y cycles per X cycle.
stages.diagnose: If you used peak-to-peak as peak pressure, or identified pitch from trace height, reread the axes. Compare the independent period and pressure measurements.
stages.repair: Mark equilibrium and extrema; recover one complete cycle on each time trace. Convert pressure-amplitude ratios to intensity only after confirming common impedance.
stages.boundary_test: If Y were measured in a different medium, what extra information is needed for intensity ratio?

core1b.fresh_task: A source gives pressure amplitudes 12 Pa at 1 m, 6 Pa at 2 m and 4 Pa at 3 m on one radial line. A second line gives 4 Pa at 2 m. Assess the ideal isotropic model and whether one radial line establishes it.
core1b.protected_work: Choose between ideal spherical spreading and an altered power-loss model using measurements at multiple distances.

stages.predict: Before fitting a model, predict whether the second radial line is compatible with the first. Record your initial reason.
stages.attempt: A source gives pressure amplitudes 12 Pa at 1 m, 6 Pa at 2 m and 4 Pa at 3 m on one radial line. A second line gives 4 Pa at 2 m. Assess the ideal isotropic model and whether one radial line establishes it.
stages.reconstruct: First line fits 1/r with product pr=12 Pa·m; second line at 2 m predicts 6 but gives 4 Pa. Global isotropy not supported; intensity ratio at 2 m is (6/4)²=2.25 between lines.
stages.diagnose: Check whether your ideal spreading prediction actually fits all locations, not merely one distance pair. What alternative loss or directional effects remain?
stages.repair: Compute pressure times distance along each comparable path, predict a third point and compare residuals. Do not infer a unique cause from failure of the ideal model.
stages.boundary_test: What additional control would distinguish directional source emission from room reflection effects?

core1b.fresh_task: Two calibrated peak-pressure traces have ratio pX/pY=2 and different frequencies. Media have unknown impedances. A student says X has four times the intensity and therefore always sounds louder. Give compatible impedance ratios that produce equality and reverse the intensity ordering, and specify a decisive observation.
core1b.protected_work: Determine whether mixed pressure and displacement evidence uniquely establishes intensity ordering, and construct physically compatible countermodels under unknown impedance or frequency.

stages.predict: Would you accept the student's intensity and loudness claims for the two pressure traces? Record separate initial verdicts.
stages.attempt: Two calibrated peak-pressure traces have ratio pX/pY=2 and different frequencies. Media have unknown impedances. A student says X has four times the intensity and therefore always sounds louder. Give compatible impedance ratios that produce equality and reverse the intensity ordering, and specify a decisive observation.
stages.reconstruct: IX/IY=4 ZY/ZX. If ZX/ZY=4, equal; if >4 (e.g. 8), IX<IY. Same impedance gives ratio 4. Measure medium impedance for each; perceived loudness also needs perceptual information.
stages.diagnose: Check if you assumed equal medium impedance or treated two different sensor quantities as interchangeable. Can an admissible change in impedance reverse your intensity ordering?
stages.repair: Choose the appropriate travelling-wave intensity relation, retain the unknown impedance, construct compatible cases and specify the measurement that would remove ambiguity. Keep loudness separate.
stages.boundary_test: If the graphs are uncalibrated voltage readings from two different microphones, what further uncertainty enters?
